reference_title: Design and Construction of Driven Pile Foundations

sections.title: Monitoring Needs Based on the Project Delivery Method, Items to Be Monitored, Review of Project Plans and Specifications, and Inspectors Tools
sections.summary: Fewer, higher resistance piles mean less redundancy, smaller tolerances and higher resistance factors, so monitoring is critical. The inspector is the owner's and engineer's eyes and ears, not a blow counter; early detection limits cost and claims. Duties differ between design-bid-build and design-build (Table 18-1); CMGC follows either. The first task is reviewing the plans and specifications and knowing the inspector's role, contacts, reports and how to flag deviations without directing the contractor.
sections.body: Chapter introduction (pp. 447-448): monitoring is only as good as the inspector's knowledge; most installation problems are avoidable with systematic inspection and good communication; problems left unattended spread to more piles and raise remediation cost, claims and delays. Sources: DFI (1995, 1997), Rausche et al. (1986), Passe (1994). 18.1 (p. 448): DBB is traditional; DB and CMGC are increasingly used; Table 18-1 compares agency duties for DBB and DB; CMGC duties may fall under either. Figure 18-1 charts the inspection process; the Contact Engineer is the agency engineer on DBB and the DB team's foundation engineer of record on DB. 18.2 (p. 448): items to monitor on every project: review of the foundation design report, plans and specifications before arriving; inspection of piles before installation; review of the contractor's pile installation plan; inspection of driving equipment before and during operation; inspection of test or indicator pile installation; inspection of production driving and maintenance of driving records. 18.3 (p. 451): understand all specified equipment, procedures and test programs, ask the originator when unclear, know the preliminary criteria and how test results adjust them; know whether the role is observational (reporting to the designer) or decision-making; whom to contact, whom to send records and daily reports to, what reports are required, and how to tell the contractor of deviations without directing the work. 18.4 (pp. 451-452): Figure 18-2 lists the inspector's tools.
key_points: Fewer, higher resistance piles: less redundancy, smaller tolerances, higher resistance factors
The inspector is the owner's and engineer's eyes and ears, more than a blow counter
Early detection and reporting limits the number of affected piles, remediation cost and claims
Table 18-1: agency duties for design-bid-build vs design-build; CMGC follows either
Monitor: design report and plans review, piles, installation plan, equipment, test piles, production piles and records
Inspector knows the role (observing or deciding), contacts, report recipients and required reports
Tell the contractor of deviations from the contract documents without directing the contractor's work

figures.title: Key components of the pile installation inspection process
figures.description: Flow chart: review plans and specifications; check the hammer and accessories are as approved; check pile type, length and material strength; confirm the driving criteria including minimum penetration; confirm field splicing procedures and inspection requirements; drive test piles to the driving criteria; inspect the hammer in operation; drive production piles to the criteria; check pile location, alignment and heave; prepare the pile installation documentation. Any 'No' leads to Contact Engineer.

tables.title: Overview of Key Construction Monitoring and Inspection Items and Agency Inspection Duties on Design-Bid-Build and Design Build Contracts
tables.description: Agency duties by item for design-bid-build and design-build: pile installation plan and hammer submittal (review plan and hammer approval analyses / submit the DB team's plan for a conformance check); test pile installation (inspect and record / observe others and communicate concerns); resistance verification (perform observations or tests / review results); driving criteria and order lengths (establish / review the DB team's); production piles (inspect and record / check piles met the criteria); foundation certification (documentation / review the DB package); verification testing (not applicable / select piles with the Engineer); piling problems (identify and coordinate resolution / document resolution).

sections.title: Inspection of Piles Prior to and During Installation
sections.summary: Specifications generally require a certificate of compliance, checked against the requirements. Timber: species, length and sizes, square butt, grain and knots, straightness, treatment, banding, shoes, splices. Precast concrete: casting yard items, then site checks (length, curing time or strength, no shipping damage, storage on blocking, cable lifting, never chain slings, pile free in the helmet, no cracks). H-piles: grade, shoes, splices, welds, flange orientation, no damage. Pipe piles: grade, wall, closure or shoes, splices, inside check before concreting.
sections.body: 18.5 (p. 452): checklists differ by pile type; obtain the certificate of compliance and compare it with the specifications; combine the pile type list here with the hammer list in 18.7. 18.5.1 (pp. 452-453): timber (ASTM D25): specified species; minimum length and toe and butt sizes, butt cut square to the axis; acceptable spiral grain twist and knots; straight; pressure treated; banding and shoes per Chapter 16; splices only if allowed. 18.5.2 (pp. 453-454): casting yard (agency inspection or a certificate): forms; spiral and strand quantity and quality with a strand certificate; splice or toe connection details and dowels cast within axial tolerance; concrete mix, slump, strength and curing; prestress forces and release time tied to transfer strength; handling, storage and curing before stripping. Site: specified length and section; a minimum wait after casting or a minimum strength; site splices to specification; no shipping or unloading damage, unloaded by slings on the cast-in lifting hooks, checked for cracks or spalling; stored above ground on blocking, kept straight; lifted with cables of adequate strength, never chain slings, frayed cables replaced, at the casting yard's pick-up points (one for short piles, two or more for long); free to twist and move laterally in the helmet; no noticeable cracks or spalling. 18.5.3 (p. 455): H-piles: grade, length and section; shoes; proprietary or full penetration splices with sections aligned; proper welds; flanges oriented per plans, since bending resistance is considerably greater perpendicular to the flanges; no head deformation. 18.5.4 (pp. 455-456): pipe piles: grade, length, wall thickness, seamless or spiral welded; closure plates or conical points of correct size properly welded, or cutting shoes; aligned splices; no damage; closed end pipes inspected for damage or water before concreting.
key_points: Obtain the certificate of compliance and compare it with the specification requirements
Timber (ASTM D25): species, length, toe and butt sizes, square butt, grain, straightness, treatment
Concrete casting yard: forms, strands, splice and toe details, concrete, prestress release, curing
Concrete at site: minimum wait after casting or minimum strength before driving
Concrete piles lifted with cables at designated pick-up points; chain slings never permitted
Concrete pile free to twist and move laterally in the helmet; no cracks or spalling
H-piles: flanges oriented per plans; bending resistance much greater perpendicular to the flanges
Closed end pipe piles inspected for damage or water before concrete filling

sections.title: Inspection of Driving Equipment and Inspection of Driving Equipment During Installation
sections.summary: Before driving check the approved hammer, hammer cushion, helmet fit and weight, concrete pile cushion (wave equation thickness, at least 4 in., new for every pile, replaced at half thickness or burning), predrilling limits and leads with a pile gate. During driving, blow count depends on hammer performance, so check each hammer type: drop hammer hoist line runs free; air/steam pressure, valve timing and racking; diesel stroke (Eq 18-1) or bounce chamber pressure and pre-ignition; hydraulic energy readouts.
sections.body: 18.6 (pp. 456-461): check the equipment against the plans before driving. Hammer: approved make and model; proper air supply and stroke; open end diesel stroke chart or electronic device; closed end diesel bounce chamber gauge calibration and energy chart; hydraulic energy or velocity display. Hammer cushion: approved material, size and thickness, fitting the helmet snugly, not excessively deformed; some air/steam hammers need a set cushion plus striker plate thickness for valve timing; measure before driving and periodically. Helmet: loose but aligned, roughly pile size, spacers discouraged, weight recorded for wave equation. Concrete pile cushion: wave equation thickness, at least 4 in.; new, not water soaked, for every pile; replaced before compressing over half its thickness, burning or charring; wood lasts about 1,000 to 2,000 blows; hard driving may need more than one. Predrilling, jetting or spudding within allowed depths, or resistance falls. Leads conform; poor alignment cuts energy and raises bending and contact stress; a centering pile gate should be required. Keep the Figure 15-50 data form on file. 18.7 (pp. 461-490): high blow counts may mean soil resistance or a poor hammer; identical models can differ. Drop: ram weight (steel 492 lb/ft3), free fall, stroke, hoist line spooling freely. Single acting air/steam: supply pressure equal to rated plus hose losses, slide bar and cams, grease, cushion stack, slack hoist line, blow rate, reduce flow gradually if racking, some warranties void above 10 blows per inch. Double acting and differential: about half the energy from downstroke pressure; keep flow so lift-off is imminent; record final pressure. Single acting diesel: exhaust ports, recoil dampener, grease every half hour, stroke by saximeter or Eq 18-1 (no jump sticks; check ram rings and the chart), fuel setting, ring compression, pre-ignition (cold hammer driving deeper; check by dynamic testing). Double acting diesel: always measure bounce chamber pressure, especially at end of driving or restrike, against the chart, corrected for batter if needed. Hydraulic: clean, warm up, power pack speed and pressure, accumulator pre-charge; on double acting models verify the ram weight in the computer and record the energy, the most important check. Resonant and vibratory: power, frequency, clamps, slack line (tight for extraction).
key_points: Hammer cushion of approved material, fitting the helmet snugly; check before driving and periodically
Record helmet weight; heavier helmets reduce energy transfer
Concrete pile cushion: wave equation thickness, at least 4 in., new for every pile; replace at half thickness or burning
Predrilling, jetting or spudding below allowed depths reduces resistance
A pile gate that centers the pile should be required
Drop hammers: hoist line must spool freely; catching the ram early cuts energy and loads the crane
Air/steam and hydraulic racking: reduce flow gradually; double acting air: half the energy from downstroke pressure
Single acting diesel stroke by saximeter or Eq 18-1 h = 4.01 (60/bpm)^2 - 0.3; no jump sticks
Pre-ignition raises blow count falsely; suspect it if a cold hammer drives deeper; check by dynamic testing
Double acting diesel: always measure bounce chamber pressure; double acting hydraulic: record the energy readout

tables.title: Common Problems and Indicators for Air/Steam Hammers
tables.description: Air/steam hammer problems and indicators: air trip malfunction (erratic rates, valve sticking); wrong cushion stack height (erratic rates); compressor pressure or volume (blow rate off specification); kinked air line (visible); moisture icing (ice at exhaust ports); no lubricant (erratic rates); worn air chest packing (slow ram, air leaking); worn nylon slide bar and ungreased columns (visible).

tables.title: Common Problems and Indicators for Single Acting Diesel Hammers
tables.description: Single acting diesel problems and indicators: water in fuel or combustion chamber (hollow sound, white smoke); clogged fuel lines (no or little gray smoke); fuel pump or injector malfunction (inconsistent strokes, gray or black smoke); low oil or oil pump malfunction (blow rate low); worn piston rings (low strokes); broken tripping device (pawl does not engage or lift); overheating (paint and oil on fins burn, sound changes).

tables.title: Common Problems and Indicators for Double Acting Diesel Hammers
tables.description: Double acting diesel problems and indicators: as for single acting diesels plus oil build-up in the bounce chamber (not visible from outside).

tables.title: Common Problems and Indicators for Single Acting Hydraulic Hammers
tables.description: Single acting hydraulic problems and indicators: hoses caught in leads (visible); leaking fittings (fluid dripping); electrical connections and sensors (erratic performance).

tables.title: Common Problems and Indicators for Double Acting Hydraulic Hammers
tables.description: Double acting hydraulic (nitrogen cap) problems and indicators: crossed hoses or wrong accumulator pressure (jumping hoses); cap pressure too high (hammer jumping on pile); low oil (erratic operation); pressure or return valve (erratic or no operation); control cable not connected (inoperable, panel bulb not lit); hoses in leads; leaking fittings; electrical connections; sensors.

sections.title: Inspection of Test or Indicator Piles and Inspection of Production Piles
sections.summary: Test piles set the criteria for all production piles and give the largest savings; problems with them repeat in production. Fourteen questions on decision authority should be settled before test driving, often at a preconstruction meeting. Production piles get a 17-item check each. Ignore the first 100 blows after a cushion change. Displacement groups go center outward or side to side, never outside in. Settlement of loose clean sands can reach 1300 ft; survey within 400 ft.
sections.body: 18.8 (pp. 490-492): small conservative foundations may have no test piles and be installed in a day or two, so inspection is the only assurance and problems (very low blow counts, refusal above scour depth, excessive lengths) must be reported quickly. Small to mid projects may have one static test or a few dynamic tests (during driving for hammer performance and stresses, on restrike for resistance), usually on the first piles. Larger projects test across the site, at the start (indicator piles for concrete order lengths) or in stages. The questions to answer before test driving: who sets test pile locations and criteria, stops driving, sets indicator pile depths, checks cutoff and heave, judges test results, orders more tests or changes, what documentation and from whom, who produces production criteria and how fast, who authorizes production and when, and whether production piles may be driven before the criteria and at whose risk. 18.9 (pp. 493-497): for each pile check type, size, length and strength; location, tolerance and orientation; splices; toe protection; plumbness; hammer; hammer cushion; pile cushion and its replacement; criteria met; unusual driving; heave; cutoff elevation; visible damage; pipe piles inspected and filled with the specified concrete and sampled; voided piles cleaned; integrity resolved; documentation complete and timely. Check blow rate against specification and record stroke, bounce chamber pressure or energy for each pile. Hammer cushions last up to 200 hours; pile cushions about 1000 to 2000 blows, replaced at half thickness or burning, no thickness changes near final driving, and blow counts used only after the first 100 blows. Keep stresses within limits (wave equation if no dynamic testing); avoid over 10 blows per inch. Compare records with adjacent piles; test suspect piles by high strain or low strain methods. Check closed pipes for water and soil, use high slump small aggregate concrete, inspect with a light or mirror. Displacement groups from the center outward or one side to the other (Figure 18-18), never outside to center; near structures drive nearest first. Woods (1997): damage uncommon beyond one pile length, but loose clean sand settlement up to 1300 ft; surveys within 400 ft, or within 0.25 times the square root of hammer energy (ft-lbs) in feet. Warm a cold hammer with about 20 blows before restrike and record each inch.
key_points: Test piles set the criteria for all production piles; the largest savings are found then
Settle 14 questions on authority, documentation and timing before test pile driving
Each production pile: 17 checks from type and location to cushions, heave, damage and documentation
Pile cushions about 1000 to 2000 blows; no thickness change near final driving; ignore first 100 blows after change
Avoid driving above 10 blows per inch by matching hammer and pile
Displacement groups: center outward or one side to the other; never outside to center
Near existing structures, drive the nearest piles first and work away
Vibration settlement of loose clean sands up to 1300 ft; preconstruction survey within 400 ft
Some specifications: survey within 0.25 x sqrt(hammer energy, ft-lbs) feet
Warm a cold hammer with about 20 blows before restrike; record restrike blows per inch

tables.title: Common Pile Installation Problems and Possible Solutions
tables.description: Problems and solutions: refusal above minimum penetration (wave equation drivability, hammer checks, dynamic measurements: pre-ignition, preadmission, soft cushion, or soil strength, relaxation, quakes, damping); driving deeper than estimated (wave equation, restrike, deeper or added piles); abrupt decrease in blow count on bearing piles (toe damage likely; reduce stroke or change hammer or section; inspect inside or test); blow count lower than expected (damage below grade, splice failure); heave or lateral movement of installed piles (redrive, change sequence, predrill); out of alignment or location tolerance (pile gate, template, fixed leads; survey as-built); shallow obstructions (excavate if within 10 ft; else spud or predrill); obstructions at depth (reduce resistance, added piles); concrete cracks in easy driving (cushion or stroke), hard driving (heavier ram, quakes), partial cracks (alignment, bending); spalling at head (cushion); steel head deforms and timber head mushrooms (helmet, evenness, banding; no acceptance from those blow counts).

sections.title: Driving Records and Reports, and Safety
sections.summary: Pile driving records list project, structure, times, contractor, hammer, cushions, pile data, elevations, blows per foot (final foot normally in blows per inch), lengths, comments and the inspector's signature; they underpin payment, engineering decisions and claims. A daily inspection report is also kept. Safety: a 100 ft pile can fall 100 ft away; plan an escape route, avoid suspended loads, the area behind the crane and in front of the pile, and standing under the hammer.
sections.body: 18.10 (pp. 502-505): records vary; most list: project identification number; project name and location; structure identification number; date and time of driving (start, stop, interruptions); contractor; hammer make, model, ram weight and energy rating, with stroke and speed whenever changed; hammer cushion and helmet weight; pile cushion and depth where changed; pile location, type, size and length; pile number matching the layout; ground, cutoff and final elevations and embedded length; blows per foot with the final foot normally in blows per inch; optional graph; cutoff length, length in ground and order length; comments and reasons for interruptions; inspector's signature and title (Figure 18-19). Records form the basis for payment and adequacy decisions and weigh heavily in claims; sloppy records encourage claims and raise cost. The daily inspection report covers equipment, work done and progress (Figure 18-20). 18.11 (p. 506): lifting and positioning piles is among the most dangerous operations; a 100 ft pile can fall 100 ft from its location, so plan an escape route; avoid the area under suspended loads, behind the crane and in front of the pile; pieces can fall from the hammer or helmet; concrete and timber piles can break and long steel piles buckle; sudden loss of resistance can break the hammer line; do not stand under the hammer marking the pile every 10 or 20 blows, but mark the pile with 1 in. marks over the expected final penetration beforehand; wear hard hat, ear and eye protection, steel toed boots, vest, harness and life jacket as conditions dictate.
key_points: Records: project and structure numbers, driving times, contractor, hammer data with stroke changes, cushions
Records: pile data, elevations, blows per foot with the final foot normally in blows per inch, signature
Driving records are the basis for payment and adequacy decisions; poor records encourage claims
Daily inspection report: equipment on site, work accomplished and progress
A 100 ft pile can fall 100 ft from its location during positioning; plan an escape route
Avoid suspended loads, the area behind the crane, in front of the pile and under the hammer
Mark the pile in 1 in. increments before driving instead of marking under the hammer
